  "chapter_body_excerpt": "# 11 Errors and projections The emergence of “madness” in Qing law, 1654-1750 Because they are produced in concrete and particular social relations, the meaning and the materiality of law are inseparable. $ ^{1} $ Previous scholarship on Qing madness laws has largely focused on the question of the “criminal responsibility” of mad people, in reference to an early scholarly debate: in riposte to an adverse review (van der Valk 1948) of his annotated translation (Bünger 1946) of important legal texts, Karl Bünger (1903-1997) maintained that “the exemption of lunatics from punishment [.... has been] a principle of the Chinese law from the Zhou dynasty until nowadays” (Bünger 1950: 8-9). This argument, based chiefly on two texts separated by more than a millennium, can be disproved with counter-examples. $ ^{2} $ More serious is the fact that even refutations have not significantly modified Bünger’s framework. Nakamura Shigeo (1973d), Martha Li Chiu (1981), Vivien Ng (1980, 1984, and 1990), and Erhard Rosner (1991) have all implied that the way the Qing legal system treated insane offenders was the system’s approach to the problem of their “criminal responsibility.” As I shall show, Qing laws that mentioned insanity applied only to killings and were not based on any principle that defined responsibility at large. Using “criminal responsibility” as a category of analysis has called disproportionate attention to minor phenomena and made significant ones more difficult to perceive.
